text: Mount Everest, known locally as Sagarmāthā in Nepal and Qomolangma in Tibet, is Earth's highest mountain above sea level and lies in the Mahalangur Himal sub-range of the Himalayas, marking part of the China–Nepal border at its summit. Its height was most recently measured in 2020 by Chinese and Nepali authorities as 8,848.86 m (29,031 ft 8+1⁄2 in). The mountain attracts many climbers, including experienced mountaineers, with two main routes: one from the southeast in Nepal (the standard route) and one from the north in Tibet. Despite not presenting substantial technical challenges on the standard route, Everest poses dangers such as altitude sickness, weather, wind, avalanches, and the Khumbu Icefall. As of May 2024, 340 people have died on Everest, and over 200 bodies remain on the mountain due to dangerous conditions. Climbers typically ascend from base camps above 5,000 m (16,404 ft), with the elevation gain varying; on the Tibetan side, climbers drive directly to the North Base Camp, while on the Nepalese side, they fly into Kathmandu, then Lukla, and trek to the South Base Camp, resulting in a climb from Lukla to the summit of about 6,000 m (20,000 ft). The first recorded attempts to reach the summit were made by British mountaineers, as Nepal restricted foreign entry. In 1921, the British reached 7,000 m (22,966 ft) on the North Col, and in 1922, they achieved the first ascent above 8,000 m (26,247 ft), pushing the North Ridge route to 8,321 m (27,300 ft). George Mallory and Andrew Irvine made a final summit attempt on 8 June 1924 but did not return, leading to debate over whether they were the first to reach the top. Tenzing Norgay and Edmund Hillary made the first documented ascent in 1953 via the Southeast Ridge route, with Norgay having reached 8,595 m (28,199 ft) in 1952 as part of a Swiss expedition. The Chinese team of Wang Fuzhou, Gonpo, and Qu Yinhua made the first reported ascent from the North Ridge on 25 May 1960. The Nepali name Sagarmāthā (IAST: Sagarmāthā, Sanskrit: Sagar-Matha, lit. "goddess of the sky") derives from सगर (sagar, "sky") and माथा (māthā, "head"). The Tibetan name Qomolangma (ཇོ་མོ་གླང་མ, lit. "holy mother") was first recorded in the 1721 Kangxi Atlas and appeared in the West in 1733 as Tchoumour Lancma on a map by D'Anville. The official Chinese transcription is Zhūmùlǎngmǎ Fēng, a phonetic rendering of the Tibetan name, adopted in May 1952 after earlier names like Shèngmǔ Fēng were phased out. The British Great Trigonometrical Survey of India, beginning in 1802, used giant theodolites weighing 500 kg (1,100 lb) and required 12 men to carry, but was hindered by Nepal's refusal to allow entry. Observations were made from Terai, where conditions were difficult due to rain and malaria, resulting in three deaths and two retirements. In 1847, Andrew Scott Waugh observed a peak beyond Kangchenjunga, designated Peak XV, and in 1849, James Nicolson made observations from 190 km (120 mi) away, with data indicating Peak XV was higher than Kangchenjunga. Radhanath Sikdar identified Peak XV as the world's highest peak in 1852 using trigonometric calculations. Waugh officially announced in 1856 that Peak XV (later named Mount Everest) was 8,840 m (29,002 ft) high, with the height rounded to 29,002 ft to avoid implying an exact value. From 1952 to 1954, the Survey of India determined the height as 8,847.73 m (29,028 ft), reaffirmed in 1975 by China at 8,848.13 m (29,029.30 ft), both measuring the snow cap, not the rock head. The 8,848 m (29,029 ft) height was officially recognized by Nepal and China. In 1999, an American expedition led by Bradford Washburn measured a rock head elevation of 8,850 m (29,035 ft) and a snow/ice elevation 1 m (3 ft) higher, though it was not officially recognized by Nepal. Geoid uncertainty questions the accuracy of both the 1999 and 2005 surveys. In 2005, the Chinese Academy of Sciences and State Bureau of Surveying and Mapping announced a height of 8,844.43 m (29,017.16 ft) with ±0.21 m (8.3 in) accuracy, based on rock height, with a snow-ice depth of 3.5 m (11 ft), and a disagreement arose over whether the official height should be rock (8,844 m) or snow (8,848 m). In 2010, both countries agreed on 8,848 m, with Nepal recognizing China's claim of a rock height of 8,844 m. On 8 December 2020, Nepal and China jointly announced the new official height as 8,848.86 m (29,031.7 ft). Plate tectonics at the Main Himalayan Thrust, where the Indian and Eurasian plates converge, are increasing Everest's height and moving the summit northeastward at rates of 4 mm (0.16 in) per year vertically and 3 to 6 mm (0.12 to 0.24 in) per year horizontally, though some accounts suggest lateral movement of 27 mm (1.1 in) or even shrinkage. The summit is the point where Earth's surface reaches the greatest distance above sea level. Mauna Kea in Hawaii is taller when measured from its base, rising over 10,200 m (33,464.6 ft) from the ocean floor, though only 4,205 m (13,796 ft) above sea level. Denali in Alaska is taller when measured from base, with a height above base of 5,600 m (18,400 ft), despite its sea-level height of 6,190 m (20,308 ft). Everest's base elevations range from 4,200 m (13,800 ft) on the south to 5,200 m (17,100 ft) on the Tibetan Plateau, giving it a height above base of 3,650 to 4,650 m (11,980 to 15,260 ft). Chimborazo in Ecuador is farther from Earth's center (6,384.4 km or 3,967.1 mi) than Everest (6,382.3 km or 3,965.8 mi) due to Earth's equatorial bulge, despite having a lower peak elevation of 6,268 m (20,564.3 ft) versus Everest's 8,848 m (29,028.9 ft). Other nearby high mountains include Lhotse (8,516 m), Nuptse (7,855 m), Changtse (7,580 m), and Khumbutse (6,636 m). The Khumbu Icefall and glacier are major obstacles on the southwest side, affecting base camps and climbs. Geologists have divided the rocks of Mount Everest into three formations.

Mount Everest, at 8,848 meters (29,028.9 feet) above sea level, is not the farthest point from Earth's center due to the planet's equatorial bulge; Chimborazo, at 6,268 meters (20,564.3 feet) above sea level, is farther from Earth's center because the Earth bulges at the equator, with a distance of 6,382.3 kilometers (3,965.8 miles) compared to Everest's 6,371.2 kilometers (3,959.0 miles). Many of the world’s highest mountains are near Everest, including Lhotse at 8,516 meters (27,940 feet), Nuptse at 7,855 meters (25,771 feet), Changtse at 7,580 meters (24,870 feet), and Khumbutse at 6,636 meters (21,772 feet). On the southwest side, the Khumbu icefall and glacier serve as a major obstacle for climbers and base camps. Geologists have divided Mount Everest’s rock layers into three formations: the Qomolangma Formation, the North Col Formation, and the Rongbuk Formation, separated by low-angle faults called detachments. The Qomolangma Formation, also known as the Jolmo Lungama Formation, extends from the summit to about 8,600 meters (28,200 feet), composed of greyish to dark grey or white, parallel laminated Ordovician limestone interlayered with recrystallized dolomite and siltstone, containing microscopic fragments of crinoids, trilobites, and ostracods; a 60-meter (200-foot) thick thrombolite bed at the foot of the "Third Step" consists of sediments bound by cyanobacteria biofilms. This formation is broken by high-angle faults ending at the Qomolangma Detachment, which separates it from the Yellow Band. The North Col Formation, from 7,000 to 8,600 meters (23,000 to 28,200 feet), includes the Yellow Band (8,200 to 8,600 meters) made of Middle Cambrian diopside-epidote marble and phyllite, with up to five percent recrystallized crinoid ossicles; the upper five meters are deformed, separated from the Qomolangma Formation by a 5–40 cm (2.0–15.7 inch) fault breccia. Below 8,200 meters, the North Col Formation consists of deformed schist and phyllite, metamorphosed from Middle to Early Cambrian deep-sea flysch. Its base is the Lhotse detachment, a regional low-angle normal fault. Below 7,000 meters, the Rongbuk Formation underlies the North Col Formation and consists of sillimanite-K-feldspar schist and gneiss intruded by leucogranite sills and dikes (1 cm to 1,500 meters thick), part of a Late Oligocene–Miocene intrusive belt formed 20 to 24 million years ago from partial melting of Paleoproterozoic to Ordovician metasedimentary rocks during Indian Plate subduction. The mountain's sedimentary and metamorphic rocks were thrust southward over the Indian Plate's Archean granulites during the Cenozoic India-Asia collision, with the Qomolangma and North Col formations originating as marine sediments from India’s continental shelf. The Rongbuk Formation formed from high-grade metamorphic and granitic rocks that were pushed down, heated, and partially melted at depths over 15 to 20 kilometers (9.3 to 12.4 miles) before being forced upward. Mount Everest is rising at about 2 mm per year. The Ordovician limestone of Everest was recognized by the International Union of Geological Sciences (IUGS) in 2022 as a geological heritage site due to its fossiliferous marine origin and international scientific relevance. Very little native flora or fauna exist on Everest; a moss grows at 6,480 meters (21,260 feet), possibly the highest altitude plant species, and Arenaria grows below 5,500 meters (18,000 feet); satellite data from 1993 to 2018 shows vegetation expansion into previously bare areas. A black jumping spider, Euophrys, has been found at up to 6,700 meters (22,000 feet), possibly the highest confirmed non-microscopic permanent resident, with E. everestensis at 5,030 meters (16,500 feet), feeding on wind-blown insects; microscopic life is likely at higher altitudes. Bar-headed geese migrate over the Himalayas and have been seen flying over Everest’s summit, with George Lowe reporting this in 1953; choughs have been spotted as high as 7,906 meters (25,938 feet) and yellow-billed choughs at 7,900 meters (25,919 feet). Yaks are used to haul gear, carrying up to 100 kilograms (220 pounds), with thick fur and large lungs; other animals include the Himalayan tahr (prey of snow leopards), Himalayan black bear (up to 4,300 meters), and red panda. A pika and ten new ant species were found in a region expedition. From Nepal, Everest is protected in Sagarmatha National Park; from China, in Qomolangma National Nature Reserve. The mountain has an ice cap climate (Köppen EF) with all months below freezing. The base camp on the Nepalese side is located on the Khumbu Glacier, which is rapidly thinning due to climate change, prompting plans by Taranath Adhikari to relocate it to a lower altitude to improve safety, though resistance from climbers and Sherpas has delayed the move due to lack of viable alternative locations. In 2008, a weather station at 8,000 meters (26,000 feet) went online, operated by SHARE, which also installed the Mount Everest webcam in 2011. The Balcony Station, at 8,430 meters (27,660 feet), is the highest weather station on Earth, set up by Tom Matthews and Baker Perry in 2019 and ceased transmitting data as of January 20, 2020. Everest extends into the upper troposphere and stratosphere, with summit air pressure about one-third of sea level; winds commonly reach 160 km/h (100 mph), with a recorded speed of 280 km/h (175 mph) in February 2004; these winds can blow climbers into chasms or reduce oxygen by up to 14 percent via Bernoulli’s principle, prompting climbers to aim for spring or fall windows when the monsoon season ends or begins. The summit was first reached by humans in 1953; only about 200 people had summited by 1987, and as of December 2024, the Himalayan Database records just under 13,000 summits by around 7,200 individuals. Early attempts include Clinton Thomas Dent suggesting climbing Everest in 1885; George Mallory and Guy Bullock discovered the northern approach in 1921, reaching 7,005 meters (22,982 feet) at the North Col, where Mallory identified a route to the summit. In 1922, Mallory, Col. Felix Norton, and Howard Somervell reached 8,225 meters (26,985 feet) without oxygen, and George Finch and Geoffrey Bruce reached 8,321 meters (27,300 feet) using oxygen. In 1924, Mallory and Geoffrey Bruce’s attempt was aborted due to weather, and Norton and Somervell reached 8,572.8 meters (28,126 feet), ascending only 30 meters in the final hour; Mallory used oxygen with Andrew Irvine, who disappeared on June 8, 1924. Mallory’s body was found in 1999 on the North Face, and Irvine’s detached foot was found in 2024, sparking debate over whether they reached the summit. In 1933, Lady Houston funded the Houston Everest Flight, where two aircraft led by the Marquess of Clydesdale flew over the summit. Early expeditions from Tibet via the North Face were unsuccessful due to access closure in 1950 after China took control of Tibet; Bill Tilman and a small party in 1950 pioneered the standard southern route through Nepal. The 1952 Swiss Mount Everest expedition was granted permission to attempt a climb.

Years before the first confirmed ascent and safe descent in 1953, Irvine's detached foot, still in a boot and sock, was found in 2024. In 1933, Lady Houston, a British millionaire, funded the Houston Everest Flight of 1933, which saw a formation of two aeroplanes led by the Marquess of Clydesdale fly over the Everest summit. Early expeditions—such as Charles Bruce's in the 1920s and Hugh Ruttledge's two unsuccessful attempts in 1933 and 1936—tried to ascend the mountain from Tibet, via the North Face. Access was closed from the north to Western expeditions in 1950 after China took control of Tibet. In 1950, Bill Tilman and a small party which included Charles Houston, Oscar Houston, and Betsy Cowles undertook an exploratory expedition to Everest through Nepal along the route which has become the standard approach to Everest from the south. The 1952 Swiss Mount Everest expedition was granted permission to attempt a climb from Nepal. It established a route through the Khumbu icefall and ascended to the South Col at an elevation of 7,986 m (26,201 ft). Raymond Lambert and Sherpa Tenzing Norgay were able to reach an elevation of about 8,595 m (28,199 ft) on the Southeast Ridge, setting a new climbing altitude record. Tenzing's experience was useful when he was hired to be part of the British expedition in 1953. The Swiss made another post-monsoon attempt in the autumn; they made it to the South Col but were driven back by winter winds and severe cold. In 1953, a ninth British expedition, led by John Hunt, returned to Nepal. Hunt selected two climbing pairs to attempt the summit. The first, Tom Bourdillon and Charles Evans, came within 100 m (330 ft) of the summit on 26 May 1953, but turned back after running into oxygen problems. As planned, their work in routefinding, breaking trail and oxygen caches were of great aid to the following pair. Two days later, the expedition made its second assault with the second pair: New Zealander Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay, a Nepali Sherpa climber. They reached the summit at 11:30 am local time on 29 May 1953 via the South Col route. At the time, both acknowledged it as a team effort by the whole expedition, but Tenzing revealed a few years later that Hillary had put his foot on the summit first. They took photos and buried sweets and a small cross in the snow before descending. On 23 May 1956, Ernst Schmied and Juerg Marmet ascended. Wang Fuzhou, Gonpo and Qu Yinhua of China made the first reported ascent of the peak from the North Ridge in May 1960. The first American to climb Everest, Jim Whittaker, joined by Nawang Gombu, reached the summit on 1 May 1963 on the American Mount Everest expedition and on 22 May on the same expedition Tom Hornbein and Willi Unsoeld were the first to traverse the mountain by climbing via the North Face and descending via the South Col. In 1970, Japanese mountaineers conducted a major expedition. The centrepiece was a large "siege"-style expedition, working on finding a new route up the Southwest Face. Another element was an attempt to ski Everest. Despite a staff of over one hundred and a decade of planning, the expedition suffered eight deaths and failed to summit. However, Japanese expeditions enjoyed some successes. Yuichiro Miura became the first man to ski down Everest from the South Col—he descended nearly 1,300 vertical metres (4,200 ft) from the South Col before falling with extreme injuries. Another success was an expedition that put four on the summit via the South Col route. Miura's exploits became the subject of film, and he went on to become the oldest person to summit Everest in 2003 aged 70 and in 2013 aged 80. In 1975, Junko Tabei became the first woman to summit Everest. The 1975 British Mount Everest Southwest Face expedition led and organised by Chris Bonington made the first ascent of the Southwest Face from the Western Cwm. In 1978, Reinhold Messner and Peter Habeler made the first ascent of Everest without supplemental oxygen. The Polish climber Andrzej Zawada headed the first winter ascent of Everest, the first winter ascent of an eight-thousander. On 15 January, the team managed to set up Camp III at 7,150 metres (23,460 ft) above sea level, but further action was stopped by hurricane-force winds. The weather improved after 11 February, when Leszek Cichy, Walenty Fiut and Krzysztof Wielicki set up camp IV on South Col at 7,906 metres (25,938 ft). Cichy and Wielicki started the final ascent at 6:50 am on 17 February. At 2:40 pm Andrzej Zawada at base camp heard the climbers' voices over the radio – "We are on the summit! The strong wind blows all the time. It is unimaginably cold." The successful winter ascent started a new decade of Winter Himalaism, which became a Polish specialisation. After 1980 Poles did ten first winter ascents on 8000 metre peaks. In 1989, Polish climbers under the leadership of Eugeniusz Chrobak organised an international expedition to Everest on a difficult western ridge. Ten Poles and nine foreigners participated, but only the Poles remained in the attempt for the summit. On 24 May, Chrobak and Andrzej Marciniak, starting from camp V at 8,200 metres (26,900 ft), overcame the ridge and reached the summit. But on 27 May, during an avalanche from the side of Khumbutse near the Lho La pass, four climbers were killed: Mirosław Dąsal, Mirosław Gardzielewski, Zygmunt Andrzej Heinrich and Wacław Otręba. The following day, due to his injuries, Chrobak died. Marciniak, who was injured, was saved by a rescue expedition in which Artur Hajzer and New Zealanders Gary Ball and Rob Hall took part. The organisation of the rescue included Reinhold Messner, Elizabeth Hawley, Carlos Carsolio and the US consul. On 10 and 11 May 1996, eight climbers died after guided expeditions were caught in a blizzard during a summit attempt on 10 May. During the 1996 season, 15 people died. These were the highest death tolls for a single weather event, and season, until the 16 deaths in the 2014 Mount Everest ice avalanche. The guiding disaster gained publicity and raised questions about the commercialisation of climbing and the safety of guiding clients on Everest. Journalist Jon Krakauer, on assignment from Outside magazine, was in one of the affected guided parties, and published the bestseller Into Thin Air, which related his experience. Krakauer was critical of guide Anatoli Boukreev. A year later, Boukreev co-authored The Climb, in part as a rebuttal of Krakauer's portrayal. The dispute sparked debate within the climbing community. Boukreev was awarded The American Alpine Club's David Sowles Award for his rescue efforts on the expedition. In 2004 researchers from the University of Toronto told the New Scientist that analysis of conditions on 11 May suggested that weather caused oxygen levels to plunge about 14 per cent. One survivor was Beck Weathers, left for dead about 275 metres (900 feet) from Camp 4 at 7,950 metres (26,085 feet). After spending a night on the mountain, Weathers made it back to Camp 4 with massive frostbite and vision impaired due to snow blindness. Fellow climbers considered his condition terminal and left him in a tent to die overnight. Weathers was lowered to Camp 2 and a helicopter rescue was organised by the Nepali Army. The storm's impact on climbers on the North Ridge, where several climbers also died, was detailed in a first-hand account by Matt Dickinson in his book The Other Side of Everest. Sixteen-year-old Mark Pfetzer was on the climb and wrote about it in Within Reach: My Everest Story. The 2015 feature film Everest is based on the events of this guiding disaster. In 2006, 12 people died. David Sharp's death triggered debate and years of discussion about climbing ethics. The question was whether climbers had left a man to die and whether he could have been saved. He attempted to summit alone with two bottles of oxygen, compared to the standard five used by most climbers. He arranged his permit through Asian Trekking, a Kathmandu-based company that provided basic services to base camp, but not beyond that point. Sharp climbed without a radio or guide. Multiple climbing parties encountered Sharp in distress. Double-amputee climber Mark Inglis said that on 15 May his climbing party, and many others, had passed Sharp, sheltering under a rock overhang 450 metres (1,480 ft) below the summit, without attempting a rescue. Inglis said 40 people had passed by Sharp, but he might have been overlooked as climbers assumed Sharp was the corpse nicknamed "Green Boots", but Inglis was not aware that climbers had tried to help Sharp despite being in the process of helping an injured woman, Burçak Özoğlu Poçan, down. There has been discussion about Himex in the commentary on Inglis and Sharp. In regard to Inglis's initial comments, he later revised details because he had been interviewed while he was "physically and mentally exhausted, and in much pain. He had suffered frostbite – he later had five fingertips amputated." It was estimated that Sharp summited on 14 May and began his descent, but on 15 May he was in trouble and being passed by climbers on their way up and down. It is believed he was suffering from hypoxia and was about 300 m (1,000 ft) from the summit on the North Side route. The Tribune, India, quoted someone who described what happened to Sharp as "the most shameful act in the history of mountaineering". Much of this controversy was captured by the Discovery Channel while filming Everest: Beyond the Limit. A crucial decision affecting Sharp is shown where a returning climber, adventurer Maxim Chaya, is descending and radios his base camp manager (Russell Brice) that he has found a frostbitten and unconscious climber in distress. Chaya is unable to identify Sharp, who had chosen to climb solo and did not identify himself to other climbers. The manager assumes Sharp is part of a group that has already calculated they must abandon him, and informs his lone climber there is no chance of him being able to help Sharp by himself. As Sharp's condition deteriorates and other descending climbers pass him, his opportunities for rescue diminish: his legs and feet curl from frostbite, preventing him walking; later descending climbers are lower on oxygen and lack the strength to offer aid; time runs out for Sherpas to return and rescue him. Sharp's body remained just below the summit on the Chinese side next to "Green Boots"; they shared a space in a rock cave that was an ad hoc tomb. Sharp's body was removed from the cave in 2007, and since 2014, Green Boots has been missing, presumably removed or buried. As the Sharp debate started, on 26 May Australian climber Lincoln Hall was found alive after being left. He was found by a party of four climbers who, giving up their own attempt, stayed with Hall and descended with him and 11 Sherpas sent up to carry him down. Hall fully recovered. His team had assumed he had died from cerebral edema, and were instructed to cover him with rocks. There were no rocks to do this and he was abandoned. The erroneous information of his death was passed to his family. On 21 May 2007, Canadian climber Meagan McGrath initiated the successful high-altitude rescue of Nepali Usha Bista. McGrath was selected as a 2011 recipient of the Sir Edmund Hillary Foundation of Canada Humanitarian Award, which recognises a Canadian who has contributed a significant service in the Himalayan Region of Nepal. By the end of 2010, there had been 5,104 summits by about 3,142 individuals, with 77 per cent accomplished since 2000. The summit was achieved in 7 of the 22 years from 1953 to 1974 and not missed between 1975 and 2014. An illustration of the explosion of popularity is provided by the number of daily ascents. Analysis of the 1996 Mount Everest disaster shows part of the blame was on the bottleneck caused by a large number of climbers (33 to 36) attempting to summit on the same day; this was unusually high at the time. By comparison, on 23 May 2010, the summit was reached by 169 climbers – more summits in a single day than in the 31 years from the first successful summit in 1953 to 1983. Nearly all attempts at the summit are done using one of two main routes. In 2005–07, more than half elected to use the more challenging, but cheaper northeast route. In 2008, the northeast route was closed by the Chinese government for the season, and the only people able to summit from the north that year were athletes carrying the Olympic torch for the 2008 Summer Olympics. The route was closed to foreigners in 2009 in the run-up to the 50th anniversary of the Dalai Lama's exile. These closures led to declining interest in the north route, and in 2010, two-thirds summitted from the south. The 2010s were a time of new highs and lows for the mountain, with disasters in 2013 and 2014 causing record deaths. In 2015 there were no summits for the first time in decades. A record was set in 2019 with over 890 summiters. On 18 April 2014, an avalanche hit the area just below Base Camp 2. 16 people were killed, all Nepali guides, and nine injured. In response, Sherpa climbing guides walked off the job and most climbing companies pulled out in respect for the Sherpa people mourning their loss. 2015 was set to be a record-breaking season of climbs, with hundreds of permits. However, on 25 April 2015, an earthquake measuring 7.8 Mw triggered an avalanche that hit Everest Base Camp, shutting down the season. 18 bodies were recovered by the Indian Army mountaineering team. The avalanche began on Pumori, moved through the Khumbu Icefall on the southwest side of Everest, and slammed into the South Base Camp. 2015 was the first time since 1974 with no spring summits, as all climbing teams pulled out. One reason for this was the high probability of aftershocks. Just weeks after the first quake, the region experienced a 7.3 quake and there were many aftershocks. The quakes trapped hundreds of climbers above the Khumbu icefall, and they had to be evacuated by helicopter as they ran low on supplies. The quake shifted the route through the ice fall, making it impassable. Bad weather made helicopter evacuation difficult. There was a large impact overall on Nepal, with 9,000 dead. In Tibet, by 28 April at least 25 had died. Hawley's database records 641 made it to the summit in early 2016. 2017 was the biggest season yet, yielding hundreds of summiters and a handful of deaths. On 27 May, Kami Rita made his 21st summit with the Alpine Ascents Everest Expedition, one of three people, along with Apa Sherpa and Phurba Tashi Sherpa to make it to the summit 21 times. The season had a tragic start with the death of Ueli Steck, who died from a fall during a warm-up climb. There was continued discussion about possible changes to the Hillary Step. Summiters for 2017 was tallied up to be 648. A record 891 summited in 2018. One factor that aided this was an especially long and clear weather window of 11 days during.

Images of hundreds queuing to reach the summit and reports of climbers stepping over dead bodies dismayed people around the world.[195][196][197] There was an announcement of an expedition to re-measure the height of Everest, particularly in light of the 2015 earthquakes.[198][199][200] Among the climbing teams was a scientific expedition with a planned study of pollution, and how things like snow and vegetation influence the availability of food and water in the region.[201] In the 2019 spring season, there were roughly 40 teams with almost 400 climbers and several hundred guides attempting to summit on the Nepali side.[202][203][204] Nepal issued 381 climbing permits for 2019.[191] For the northern routes in Chinese Tibet, several hundred more permits were issued.[205] In May, Nepali mountaineering guide Kami Rita summited twice within a week, his 23rd and 24th ascents.[206][202][203] By 28 May, the death toll reached 11, when a climber died at about 7,900 m (26,000 ft) during the descent,[193] and a 12th climber was missing and later declared dead.[194] The deaths were possibly due to crowding leading to delays high on the mountain, and shorter weather windows.[191] Someone who had summited previously noted that when the weather window opens, long lines form as everyone rushes to summit and get back down.[207][208] Despite the number of deaths, reports indicated that a record 891 climbers summited in the spring 2019 climbing season.[209][159] Although China has had permit restrictions, and Nepal requires a doctor to sign off on climbing permits,[209] the natural dangers of climbing such as falls and avalanches combined with medical issues aggravated by Everest's extreme altitude led to 2019 being a year with a comparatively high death toll.[209] Both Nepal and China prohibited foreign climbing groups during the 2020 season, due to the COVID-19 pandemic. 2020 saw no summits from the Nepal (South) Side.[210] In October 2025, blizzard-like conditions prompted Chinese authorities to evacuate nearly 350 people by October 6, with about 200 more stranded on the Everest Scenic Area.[211][212] In 2014, Nepal issued 334 climbing permits, which were extended until 2019 due to the closure.[214] In 2015, Nepal issued 357 permits, but the mountain was closed again because of the avalanche and earthquake, and these permits were given a two-year extension to 2017.[215][214] In 2017, a person who tried to climb Everest without the $11,000 permit was caught after he made it past the Khumbu icefall. He faced, among other penalties, a $22,000 fine and a possible four years in jail. In the end, he was allowed to return home but banned from mountaineering in Nepal for 10 years.[216] The number of permits issued each year by Nepal is:[215][217] The Chinese side in Tibet is also managed with permits for summiting Everest.[220] They did not issue permits in 2008, due to the Olympic torch relay being taken to the summit of Mount Everest.[221] In March 2020, the governments of China and Nepal cancelled all climbing permits for Mount Everest due to the COVID-19 pandemic.[222][223] In April 2020, a group of Chinese mountaineers began an expedition from the Chinese side. The mountain remained closed on the Chinese side to all foreign climbers.[224] On 10 May 2021, a separation line was announced by Chinese authorities to prevent the spread of coronavirus from climbers ascending Nepal's side.[225] According to Jon Krakauer, the era of commercialisation of Everest started in 1985, when the summit was reached by a guided expedition led by David Breashears that included Richard Bass, a wealthy 55-year-old businessman and an amateur mountain climber with four years of climbing experience.[227] By the early-1990s, several companies were offering guided tours to the mountain. Rob Hall, one of the mountaineers who died in the 1996 disaster, had successfully guided 39 clients to the summit before that incident.[228]: 24, 42  By 2016, most guiding services cost between US$35,000 and US$200,000.[229] Going with a "celebrity guide", usually a well-known mountaineer typically with decades of climbing experience and perhaps several Everest summits, can cost over £100,000 as of 2015.[230] However, the services offered vary widely and it is "buyer beware" when doing deals in Nepal, one of the poorest and least developed countries in the world.[229][231] Tourism contributed 7.9 per cent of the gross domestic product (GDP) in 2019[232] in a country with high unemployment,[233] but an Everest porter can make nearly double the nation's average wage in a region in which other sources of income are lacking.[234] Costs beyond the guiding service can vary widely. It is technically possible to reach the summit with minimal additional expenses, and there are "budget" travel agencies that offer logistical support for such trips. A limited support service, offering only some meals at base camp and bureaucratic overhead like a permit, can cost as little as US$7,000 as of 2007.[148] However, this is considered difficult and dangerous (as illustrated by the case of David Sharp).[235] Climbing gear required to reach the summit may cost in excess of US$8,000, and most climbers also use bottled oxygen, which adds around US$3,000.[236] The permit to enter the Everest area from the south via Nepal costs US$10,000 to US$30,000 per person, depending on the size of the team.[236] The ascent typically starts at one of the two base camps near the mountain, both of which are approximately 100 kilometres (60 mi) from Kathmandu and 300 kilometres (190 mi) from Lhasa (the two nearest cities with major airports). Transferring one's equipment from the airport to the base camp may add as much as US$2,000.[236] Many climbers hire "full service" guide companies, which provide a wide spectrum of services, including the acquisition of permits, transportation to/from base camp, food, tents, fixed ropes,[237] medical assistance while on the mountain, an experienced mountaineer guide, and even personal porters to carry one's backpack and cook one's meals. The cost of such a guide service may range from US$40,000 to $80,000 per person.[238] Since most equipment is moved by Sherpas, clients of full-service guide companies can often keep their backpack weights under 10 kilograms (22 lb), or hire a Sherpa to carry their backpack for them. By contrast, climbers attempting less commercialised peaks, like Denali, are often expected to carry backpacks over 30 kilograms (66 lb) and, occasionally, to tow a sled with 35 kilograms (77 lb) of gear and food.[239] The degree of commercialisation of Mount Everest is a frequent subject of criticism.[177] Jamling Tenzing Norgay, the son of Tenzing Norgay, said in a 2003 interview that his late father would have been shocked to discover that rich thrill-seekers with no climbing experience were now routinely reaching the summit, "You still have to climb this mountain yourself with your feet. But the spirit of adventure is not there any more. It is lost. There are people going up there who have no idea how to put on crampons. They are climbing because they have paid someone $65,000. It is very selfish. It endangers the lives of others."[240] One example of this is Shriya Shah-Klorfine, who had to be taught how to put on crampons during her summit attempt in 2012.[241] She paid at least US$40,000 to a new guiding company for the trip, and died when she ran out of oxygen during the descent after climbing for 27 hours straight.[242] Reinhold Messner concurred in 2004: 
You could die in each climb and that meant you were responsible for yourself. We were real mountaineers: careful, aware and even afraid. By climbing mountains we were not learning how big we were. We were finding out how breakable, how weak and how full of fear we are. You can only get this if you expose yourself to high danger. I have always said that a mountain without danger is not a mountain....High altitude alpinism has become tourism and show. These commercial trips to Everest, they are still dangerous. But the guides and organisers tell clients, 'Don't worry, it's all organised.' The route is prepared by hundreds of Sherpas. Extra oxygen is available in all camps, right up to the summit. People will cook for you and lay out your beds. Clients feel safe and don't care about the risks.[243] By 2015, Nepal was considering requiring that climbers have some experience, hoping this would both make the mountain safer and increase revenue.[244] One barrier to this is that low-budget firms make money not taking inexperienced climbers to the summit.[229] Those turned away by Western firms can often find another firm willing to take them for a price—that they return home soon after arriving after base camp, or part way up the mountain.[229] However, not all opinions on the subject among prominent mountaineers have been strictly negative. For example, Edmund Hillary stated in 2003 that while "Having people pay $65,000 and then be led up the mountain by a couple of experienced guides...isn't really mountaineering at all",[245] he was pleased by the changes brought to Everest area by Westerners: 
I don't have any regrets because I worked very hard indeed to improve the condition for the local people. When we first went in there they didn't have any schools, they didn't have any medical facilities, all over the years we have established 27 schools, we have two hospitals and a dozen medical clinics and then we've built bridges over wild mountain rivers and put in fresh water pipelines so in cooperation with the Sherpas we've done a lot to benefit them.[246] One of the early guided summiters, Richard Bass (of Seven Summits fame) stated in 2003 that "Climbers should have high altitude experience before they attempt the really big mountains. People don't realise the difference between a 20,000-foot [6,100 m] mountain and 29,000-foot [8,800 m]. It's not just arithmetic. The reduction of oxygen in the air is proportionate to the altitude alright, but the effect on the human body is disproportionate—an exponential curve. People climb Denali [6,190 m or 20,320 ft] or Aconcagua [6,960 m or 22,834 ft] and think, 'Heck, I feel great up here, I'm going to try Everest.' But it's not like that."[247] Some expedition teams have clients use altitude tents to pre-acclimatise prior to leaving for the mountain. Compared to traditional Everest expeditions that last 50 to 60 days, altitude tents can reduce the expedition time frame to 30 to 35 days.[248] In 2025, four men climbed the mountain in one week. They claimed their inhalation of xenon gas 10 days prior to stimulate erythropoietin production had eliminated the need for altitude acclimatisation over several weeks. The International Climbing and Mountaineering Federation (UIAA) criticised the decision, citing that there is no evidence that the inhalation of xenon improves performance in high elevation environments. Furthermore, the UIAA warned that as an anesthetic, xenon gas could result in impaired brain function, respiratory compromise, and death if used in an unmonitored setting.[249][250][251] Summiting Everest with disabilities has become popular in the 21st century. Sudarshan Gautam, a Canadian double-amputee, summited the mountain in 2013.[252] In the same year, Eli Reimer, a teenager with Down syndrome, hiked to the South Base Camp as part of a fundraising effort for his father's foundation.[253] Mount Everest has two main climbing routes, the Southeast Ridge from Nepal and the North Ridge from Tibet, as well as many other less frequently climbed routes.[254] Of the two main routes, the Southeast Ridge is technically easier and more frequently used. It was the route used by Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay in 1953 and the first recognised of 15 routes to the top by 1996.[254] This was, however, a route decision dictated more by politics than by design, as the Chinese border was closed to the western world in the 1950s, after Annexation of Tibet by the People's Republic of China.[255] Most attempts are made during May, before the summer monsoon season. As the monsoon season approaches, the jet stream shifts northward, thereby reducing the average wind speeds high on the mountain.[256][257] While attempts are sometimes made in September and October, after the monsoons, when the jet stream is again temporarily pushed northward, the additional snow deposited by the monsoons and the less stable weather patterns at the monsoons' tail end makes climbing extremely difficult. The ascent via the Southeast Ridge begins with a trek to Base Camp at 5,380 m (17,700 ft) on the south side of Everest, in Nepal. Expeditions usually fly into Lukla (2,860 m) from Kathmandu and pass through Namche Bazaar. Climbers then hike to Base Camp, which usually takes six to eight days, allowing for proper altitude acclimatisation in order to prevent altitude sickness.[258] Climbing equipment and supplies are carried by yaks, dzopkyos (yak-cow hybrids), and human porters to Base Camp on the Khumbu Glacier. When Hillary and Tenzing climbed Everest in 1953, the British expedition they were part of (comprising over 400 climbers, porters, and Sherpas at that point) started from the Kathmandu Valley, as there were no roads further east at that time. Climbers spend a couple of weeks in Base Camp, acclimatising to the altitude. During that time, Sherpas and some expedition climbers set up ropes and ladders in the treacherous Khumbu Icefall. Seracs, crevasses, and shifting blocks of ice make the icefall one of the most dangerous sections of the route. Many climbers and Sherpas have been killed in this section. To reduce the hazard, climbers usually begin their ascent well before dawn, when the freezing temperatures glue ice blocks in place. Above the icefall is Camp I at 6,065 metres (19,900 ft). From Camp I, climbers make their way up the Western Cwm to the base of the Lhotse Face, where Camp II or Advanced Base Camp (ABC) is established at 6,500 m (21,300 ft). The Western Cwm is a flat, gently rising glacial valley, marked by huge lateral crevasses in the centre, which prevent direct access to the upper reaches of the Cwm. Climbers are forced to cross on the far right, near the base of Nuptse, to a small passageway known as the "Nuptse corner". The Western Cwm is also called the "Valley of Silence" as the topography of the area generally cuts off wind from the climbing route. The high altitude and a clear, windless day can make the Western Cwm unbearably hot for climbers.[259] From Camp II, climbers ascend the Lhotse Face on fixed ropes.

Sherpas have been killed in this section of Mount Everest, prompting climbers to begin their ascent well before dawn to reduce hazards, as freezing temperatures glue ice blocks in place. Above the icefall is Camp I at 6,065 metres (19,900 ft). From Camp I, climbers proceed up the Western Cwm to the base of the Lhotse Face, where Camp II or Advanced Base Camp (ABC) is established at 6,500 m (21,300 ft). The Western Cwm is a flat, gently rising glacial valley with large lateral crevasses in the center, preventing direct access; climbers cross near the base of Nuptse to a passage called the "Nuptse corner." This area is known as the "Valley of Silence" due to its windless conditions, though high altitude and clear, still air can make it unbearably hot. From Camp II, climbers ascend the Lhotse Face on fixed ropes to Camp III at 7,470 m (24,500 ft), then another 500 metres to Camp IV on the South Col at 7,920 m (26,000 ft). Between Camp III and Camp IV, climbers face the Geneva Spur—an anvil-shaped black rock named by the 1952 Swiss expedition—and the Yellow Band, a section of interlayered marble, phyllite, and semischist requiring about 100 metres of rope. On the South Col, climbers enter the death zone, where they typically endure no more than two or three days; if weather is poor with high winds, they must descend, often back to Base Camp. From Camp IV, climbers begin their summit push around midnight, aiming to reach the summit (another 1,000 metres above) within 10 to 12 hours. They first reach "The Balcony" at 8,400 m (27,600 ft), a small platform for rest and viewing, then climb over a series of imposing rock steps that force them into waist-deep snow, a serious avalanche hazard. At 8,750 m (28,700 ft), a small table-sized dome of ice and snow marks the South Summit. From there, climbers follow the knife-edge Southeast Ridge, known as the "Cornice traverse," where snow clings to rock; a misstep to the left would send one 2,400 m (7,900 ft) down the Southwest Face, while to the right is the 3,050 m (10,010 ft) Kangshung Face. At 8,790 m (28,840 ft), the 12 m (39 ft) rock wall known as the Hillary Step is encountered. Hillary and Tenzing were the first to ascend it using primitive ice climbing equipment; today, climbers use fixed ropes set up by Sherpas. Above the step, the climb to the summit is moderately angled snow slopes, though exposure is extreme, especially on large snow cornices. With increasing numbers climbing, the Step has become a bottleneck, causing long waits. After the Step, climbers traverse a loose, rocky section with fixed ropes that can be problematic in bad weather; they typically spend less than half an hour at the summit to descend to Camp IV before darkness or due to running out of oxygen. The North Ridge route begins in Tibet, with expeditions trekking to the Rongbuk Glacier and setting up base camp at 5,180 m (16,990 ft). To reach Camp II, climbers ascend the medial moraine of the east Rongbuk Glacier to the base of Changtse at around 6,100 m (20,000 ft). Camp III (ABC) is located below the North Col at 6,500 m (21,300 ft). Climbers ascend to the North Col at 7,010 m (23,000 ft) via fixed ropes, then climb the rocky North Ridge to Camp V at around 7,775 m (25,500 ft), crossing the North Face diagonally to Camp VI at 8,230 m (27,000 ft) before making the final summit push. Climbers face a treacherous traverse from the base of the First Step (8,501 to 8,534 m / 27,890 to 28,000 ft) to the Second Step (8,577 to 8,626 m / 28,140 to 28,300 ft), which includes the "Chinese ladder," a semi-permanent metal ladder placed in 1975 by Chinese climbers and used by virtually all climbers. After the Second Step, the Third Step (8,690 to 8,800 m / 28,510 to 28,870 ft) is climbed, followed by a 50-degree snow slope to the summit ridge. The summit is described as "the size of a dining room table," capped with snow over ice over rock, with snow layer variation from year to year; the rock summit is made of Ordovician limestone, a low-grade metamorphic rock. Below the summit is "rainbow valley," filled with dead bodies in brightly coloured gear, and down to about 8,000 m (26,000 ft) lies the "death zone" due to low oxygen and high danger. At these high altitudes, temperatures can drop to very low levels, causing frostbite, and snow is well-frozen, leading to slipping and falling. High winds are also a threat. Atmospheric pressure at the summit is about 0.333 standard atmospheres (337 mbar), providing only about a third as much oxygen. A sea-level dweller exposed to altitudes above 8,500 m (27,900 ft) without acclimatisation would lose consciousness in two to three minutes. Blood oxygen saturation drops from 98–99% at sea level to 85–87% at base camp and very low levels at the summit, resulting in breathing rates of 80–90 breaths per minute, leading to exhaustion. Lack of oxygen, exhaustion, extreme cold, and climbing hazards contribute to the death toll; injured climbers are often left behind, and as of 2015, over 200 bodies remain on the mountain. Debilitating symptoms of high-altitude cerebral oedema commonly appear during descent, with profound fatigue and late summit times linked to death. A 2008 study found most deaths occur in the death zone, especially during descent. A 2014 article noted that while falling is a major danger for all 8000ers, avalanches are more common at lower altitudes. Despite this, Everest is safer than peaks like Kangchenjunga, K2, Annapurna, Nanga Parbat, and Eiger (especially the nordwand) in some measures, depending on the period. Factors affecting lethality include mountain popularity, climber skill, and climb difficulty. Retinal haemorrhages, affecting up to a quarter of climbers, can damage eyesight and cause blindness; in 2010, a climber went blind and died in the death zone. A team tried to rescue a climber who became incapacitated but failed due to difficult terrain. Rescuing someone who is incapacitated is extremely difficult, and in 2011, two Nepali men paraglided off the summit after running out of oxygen and supplies, descending to Namche Bazaar in 42 minutes. Most expeditions use oxygen masks and tanks above 8,000 m (26,247 ft); while Everest can be climbed without oxygen, only the most accomplished climbers do so, and the death rate is double for those who attempt it without supplemental oxygen. Travelling above 8,000 m causes cerebral hypoxia; one study found that Mount Everest may be the highest an acclimatised human can reach, but climbers may suffer permanent neurological damage despite returning to lower altitudes. The use of bottled oxygen was first used in 1922 by George Finch and Geoffrey Bruce, who climbed to 8,100 m (26,600 ft) at 270 m/h (900 ft/h) with oxygen, though the Alpine world initially rejected it as unsportsmanlike. George Mallory later concluded that he could not summit without it and used oxygen in his 1924 attempt. When Tenzing and Hillary reached the summit in 1953, they used open-circuit oxygen, and Griffith Pugh called the debate a "futile controversy," noting oxygen enhances the climber's appreciation of surroundings. For 25 years, bottled oxygen was standard for summit success. Reinhold Messner became the first to climb Everest without oxygen in 1978 with Peter Habeler, and in 1980 he summited solo without oxygen or support on the northwest route. After the climbing community accepted oxygen-free ascents, many purists insisted it should be the norm. The 1996 disaster intensified the debate; Jon Krakauer criticized oxygen use, arguing it allowed unqualified climbers to attempt the summit, leading to dangerous situations and more deaths. The disaster was partly caused by 34 climbers attempting the ascent, causing bottlenecks at the Hillary Step and delays beyond the usual 14:00 turnaround. Krakauer proposed banning oxygen except in emergencies to reduce pollution and keep only qualified climbers on the mountain. The guide Anatoli Boukreev's decision not to use oxygen was criticized by Krakauer, who argued that without oxygen, Boukreev could not assist clients in descending; supporters claim oxygen gives a false sense of security. Low oxygen causes cognitive impairment, described as "bradypsychia," and in severe cases, hallucinations; some studies show altered brain structure in high-altitude climbers. Everest is also climbed in autumn (post-monsoon season), such as in 2010 when Eric Larsen and five Nepali guides summited after a ten-year gap; autumn is considered more dangerous due to unstable new snow, though it attracts winter sports like skiing and snowboarding. Two Japanese climbers summited in October 1973, and Chris Chandler and Bob Cormack did so in October 1976 as part of the American Bicentennial Expedition, the first American autumn ascent. By the 21st century, summer and autumn have become more popular for skiing and snowboarding. In the 1980s, autumn climbing was more popular than spring. U.S. astronaut Karl Gordon Henize died in October 1993 on an autumn expedition conducting a radiation experiment. Winter climbing is not popular due to cold, high winds, and short days; by January, summit winds reach 270 km/h (170 mph) and temperatures average −33°F (−36°C). Some climbers have reported life-threatening thefts from supply caches. In May 20, the document is cut off.

Chris Chandler and Bob Cormack reached the summit of Mount Everest in October 1976 as part of the American Bicentennial Everest Expedition, becoming the first Americans to make an autumn ascent of the mountain, as reported by the Los Angeles Times. By the 21st century, summer and autumn have become more popular for skiing and snowboarding attempts on Everest. During the 1980s, autumn climbing was more popular than spring climbing. U.S. astronaut Karl Gordon Henize died in October 1993 during an autumn expedition, conducting a radiation experiment, as background radiation increases with higher altitudes. Mount Everest has also been climbed in winter, but this is not popular due to extreme cold, high winds, and short days; by January, the peak is typically exposed to 270 km/h (170 mph) winds and has an average summit temperature of −33 °F (−36 °C). Some climbers have reported life-threatening thefts from supply caches; in May 2006, Vitor Negrete, the first Brazilian to climb Everest without oxygen and a member of David Sharp's party, died during descent, and theft of gear and food from his high-altitude camp may have contributed. Michael Kodas, in his 2008 book *High Crimes: The Fate of Everest in an Age of Greed*, described unethical guides and Sherpas, prostitution and gambling at the Tibet Base Camp, fraud in oxygen bottle sales, and climbers collecting donations falsely claiming to remove trash. In 2007, the Chinese side of Everest was described as "out of control" after a Canadian had all his gear stolen and was abandoned by his Sherpa, though another Sherpa helped him escape safely and provided spare gear; other climbers have also reported missing oxygen bottles, which can be worth hundreds of dollars each, and hundreds of climbers pass by tents, making theft difficult to prevent; reports of oxygen bottle theft became more common in the late 2010s. By the end of the 2010 climbing season, there had been 5,104 ascents by about 3,142 individuals. Notable firsts include Lucy, Lady Houston, who funded the Houston Everest Flight of 1933, where a formation of airplanes led by the Marquess of Clydesdale flew over the summit to photograph the terrain. On 26 September 1988, Jean-Marc Boivin made the first paraglider descent of Everest via the Southeast Ridge, setting records for the fastest descent and the highest paraglider flight; he noted he was tired due to trail damage and difficulty running at that altitude. In 1991, four men in two balloons achieved the first hot-air balloon flight over Everest; one balloon carried Andy Elson and Eric Jones, the other Chris Dewhirst and Leo Dickinson, who later wrote a book titled *Ballooning Over Everest*; the balloons were modified to operate up to 12,000 m (40,000 ft); Reinhold Messner called one of Dickinson’s Kodachrome photos the "best snap on Earth"; Dewhirst offered to take passengers on a repeat for $2.6 million per person. In May 2005, French pilot Didier Delsalle landed a Eurocopter AS350 B3 on the summit to set FAI records for the highest landing and take-off, staying for about four minutes, twice; he had also landed on the South Col two days earlier, and the landing was confirmed by the FAI; during the flight, he rescued two Japanese climbers at 4,880 m (16,000 ft), with one noting the record improved rescue chances. On 21 May 2011, Nepali climbers Lakpa Tsheri Sherpa and Sano Babu Sunuwar paraglided from the summit to Namche Bazaar in 42 minutes, then hiked, biked, and kayaked to the Indian Ocean, reaching the Bay of Bengal by 27 June 2011, becoming the first people to complete a continuous summit-to-sea descent; Babu had never climbed before, and Lakpa had never kayaked or swam; the duo won National Geographic Adventurers of the Year in 2012; footage of the flight was shown on Nightline in 2013. In 2014, mountaineer Wang Jing led a team that used a helicopter to fly from South Base Camp to Camp II to avoid the Khumbu Icefall and then climbed to the summit, sparking controversy over the legitimacy and propriety of the climb; Nepal investigated her, and she initially denied flying to Camp II, admitting only that support crew were flown there, but later stated in August 2014 that she had flown to Camp II because the icefall was impassable, saying, "If you don't fly to Camp II, you just go home," and insisting she had not hidden the fact; her team used the south side because the Chinese denied them a permit, and this refusal may have benefited Nepal by allowing it to showcase improved hospitals and promote a hybrid aviation/mountaineering style, sparking discussions about helicopter use; National Geographic noted a village honored Wang with awards after she donated $30,000 to the town’s hospital; she won the International Mountaineer of the Year Award from Nepal in June 2014. In 2016, increased helicopter use was noted for greater efficiency and for hauling supplies over the deadly Khumbu Icefall, saving icefall porters 80 trips but still increasing commercial activity; after many deaths in the icefall in 2014, the Nepali government wanted helicopters to transport climbers to Camp 1, but this was blocked by the 2015 earthquake, so it was implemented in 2016 (helicopters were instrumental in rescues in 2015); in that summer, Bell tested the 412EPI, which hovered at 5,500 m (18,000 ft) and flew as high as 6,100 m (20,000 ft) near Everest. Mount Everest has hosted winter sports and adventures such as skiing, snowboarding, paragliding, and BASE jumping. Yuichiro Miura became the first man to ski down Everest in the 1970s, descending nearly 1,300 vertical meters (4,200 ft) from the South Col before falling with severe injuries; Stefan Gatt and Marco Siffredi snowboarded Everest in 2001; other skiers include Davo Karničar of Slovenia, who descended from the top to South Base Camp in 2000, Hans Kammerlander of Italy in 1996 on the north side, and Kit DesLauriers of the United States in 2006; Marco Siffredi died in 2002 during a second snowboarding expedition; in 2025, Andrzej Bargiel completed the first ski descent of Everest without supplemental oxygen. Gliding descents have become more popular, noted for rapid descents; in 1986, Steve McKinney led an Everest expedition; in 1988, Jean-Marc Boivin made the first paraglider descent from the Southeast Ridge to a lower camp; in 2011, Sano Babu Sunuwar and Lakpa Tsheri Sherpa made a gliding descent from the summit down 5,000 meters (16,400 ft) in 45 minutes. The southern part of Mount Everest is considered one of several "hidden valleys" of refuge designated by Padmasambhava, a ninth-century Buddhist saint. Near the north side of Everest lies Rongbuk Monastery, described as the "sacred threshold to Mount Everest" with dramatic views; it is a key pilgrimage site for Sherpas in the Khumbu region, accessible via Nangpa La. Miyolangsangma, a Tibetan Buddhist "Goddess of Inexhaustible Giving," is believed to reside at the top of Everest; Sherpa Buddhist monks believe Everest is her palace and playground, and climbers are only partially welcome guests who arrive without invitation. Sherpas believe the mountain and its slopes are blessed with spiritual energy, and one should show reverence when passing through, as karmic effects are magnified and impure thoughts are discouraged. In 2015, the president of the Nepal Mountaineering Association warned that pollution, especially human waste, had reached critical levels; up to 12,000 kg (26,500 lb) of human excrement is left behind each season; waste is scattered along the route, making sleeping areas minefields; climbers above Base Camp typically bury waste in snow, sling it into crevasses, or defecate where convenient, often within meters of their tents; the only safe place to defecate without contaminating the mountain is Base Camp, located at approximately 5,500 m (18,000 ft), which sees the most activity; in the late 1990s, expeditions began using toilets made from blue plastic 190-liter (50-US-gallon) barrels with seats and enclosures. The waste problem is worsened by non-human waste such as used oxygen tanks, abandoned tents, and empty cans and bottles; the Nepali government now requires each climber to pack out eight kilograms of waste when descending. In February 2019, China closed the base camp on its side of Everest to visitors without climbing permits, allowing tourists to go only as far as Rongbuk Monastery. In April 2019, the Khumbu Pasanglhamu Rural Municipality launched a campaign to collect nearly 10,000 kg (20,000 lb) of garbage from Everest; in 2024, waste removal continues to receive attention.
